leads.title: Steam trawling in the North Sea
leads.where: North Shields, Grimsby and Hull, England
leads.date: 1877 (first steam tug trawling); purpose-built steam trawlers from 1881
leads.why: Engine-powered trawlers multiplied catches, made fresh sea fish cheap city food and began the industrial fishing that has depleted stocks worldwide.
leads.verify: The first steam trawling at North Shields and the first purpose-built steam trawlers; the otter trawl of the 1890s; the much older sailing beam trawl; the factory freezer trawler of 1954 as the next step.

leads.title: Net-pen salmon farming in Norway
leads.where: Hitra and the western Norwegian coast
leads.why: Raising salmon in floating sea cages started the industrial marine fish farming that now supplies more fish than capture does for many species.
leads.verify: The first successful sea-cage salmon farms and who built them; the earlier Norwegian trout trials and the Japanese yellowtail net cages of the 1950s that the method drew on.

leads.title: Mounted bison hunting on the Great Plains
leads.where: Great Plains of North America (Comanche, Lakota, Blackfoot and neighbouring peoples)
leads.why: Plains peoples took the Spanish horse and built a new way of life on it, following and running down bison herds on horseback in place of the older communal drives on foot.
leads.verify: When horses reached each Plains people, since recent archaeological and genomic work puts their spread before the Pueblo Revolt of 1680; how the mounted chase changed hunting, mobility and trade. Mounted hunting is far older in Eurasia, so this is a derived origin. The communal foot drives it replaced (jumps and pounds from c. 3700 BCE at Head-Smashed-In) have no record yet.

leads.title: Turkey husbandry in Mesoamerica
leads.where: Central Mexico and the Maya lowlands
leads.why: The turkey was the only large animal domesticated in Mesoamerica, kept for meat, feathers and ritual, and was carried worldwide after 1500.
leads.verify: The earliest remains of managed turkeys in Mesoamerica (El Mirador and central Mexican sites) and their dates; the separate domestication of turkeys in the south-western United States shown by ancient DNA, which may deserve its own record.

leads.title: Stingless beekeeping among the Maya
leads.where: Yucatán peninsula and the Maya lowlands
leads.why: The Maya kept native stingless bees in log hives for honey, wax and ritual drink, a tradition that continues in Yucatán.
leads.verify: The earliest physical or pictorial evidence of kept stingless bees (the ceramic hive from Nakum, hive-shaped stone discs, the Madrid Codex) and its date.

leads.title: Systematic livestock breeding in the English Midlands
leads.why: Bakewell's selection, inbreeding and progeny testing produced fast-maturing meat breeds, started pedigree breeding and herd books, and gave Darwin his model of selection.
leads.verify: What Bakewell did that earlier breeders had not (close inbreeding, letting sires out for progeny testing, selecting for carcass); measured changes in sheep and cattle; earlier deliberate breeding traditions, such as Arab horse breeding, that would qualify first_known.

concepts.name: Aquaculture
concepts.summary: Raising and managing fish or other aquatic animals in enclosed or controlled waters.

concepts.name: Beekeeping
concepts.summary: Housing colonies of bees in made hives so that honey and wax can be harvested repeatedly.

concepts.name: Livestock herding
concepts.summary: Managing animal populations for human use through care, confinement or movement.

concepts.name: Mechanised trawling
concepts.summary: Towing a bag net along the seabed or through the water with an engine-driven vessel.

concepts.name: Mounted hunting
concepts.summary: Pursuing and killing large game from the back of a ridden animal.

concepts.name: Systematic animal breeding
concepts.summary: Improving livestock deliberately by selecting and recording parents for measured traits and mating close relatives to fix them.
